title: API authentication and partner API key management
status_rationale: Echelon has no production deployment; the relevant rules exist only in the proposed Secure Construction Standard v0.1 or Unbound requirements, so this is a target state.
target_answer: Partner and service integrations authenticate with tenant-bound, least-privilege credentials issued through a managed identity provider, preferably OAuth client credentials with sender-constrained tokens (mutual TLS or DPoP) for money-relevant operations; static API keys, where a partner requires them, are scoped, expiring, stored only as hashes, rotatable without downtime and visible with last-use data to the sponsor. Revocation takes effect within minutes and is evidenced.

challenge.customer_intent: Ensure only the intended partner system can act through the API, and that a leaked credential has limited and short-lived value.
challenge.adverse_outcome: Stolen partner key used to read donor data or submit fraudulent requests.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: Static bearer API keys with periodic rotation are common but leak through logs, repositories and partner systems; rotation schedules rarely limit real exposure.
challenge.legally_required: No specific mechanism is mandated; FFIEC authentication guidance and GLBA safeguards expect risk-appropriate authentication.
challenge.contractually_required: Partners often ask for API keys and fixed rotation periods.
challenge.historical_convention: Long-lived API key plus IP allowlist plus 90-day rotation.
challenge.architectural_elimination: Sender-constrained tokens make a stolen token useless without the private key; short-lived tokens limit replay.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Gateway rejects unbound or expired tokens; credential inventory alerts on unused or overdue credentials.
challenge.continuous_evidence: Credential inventory with last-use and scope, revocation events.
challenge.stronger_alternative: OAuth client credentials with mTLS or DPoP binding and short token lifetimes.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Yes, configuration and token validation tests are reproducible.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Unknown; unvalidated. The prior agent judgment is kept in supporting_arguments.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: A fallback static key path left enabled for all partners.
challenge.alternative_cost: Higher partner onboarding effort and certificate management.
supporting_arguments: Removes the value of leaked credentials.
Aligns with OAuth security best practice.

agent judgment: customer acceptance likelihood 'Likely for technically mature partners; smaller partners may lack mTLS or DPoP support.'; institutional acceptance rating 'likely' (unvalidated, no cited source).
opposing_arguments: Partner capability varies; dual paths increase complexity.

Institutional acceptance is unvalidated: no buyer, auditor, regulator or insurer evidence or cited source supports an acceptance rating (DD-VAL-ADV-001, DD-VAL-ADV-002). Treat any rating as agent judgment until target-customer conversations or a sourced document support it.

title: Webhooks, inbound events and consumption of third-party APIs
status_rationale: Echelon has no production deployment; the relevant rules exist only in the proposed Secure Construction Standard v0.1 or Unbound requirements, so this is a target state.
target_answer: Outbound webhooks are signed with per-partner rotating keys and include timestamps and event identifiers; inbound events are verified, checked against a replay window, deduplicated, schema-validated and treated as untrusted data that cannot by itself grant sponsor approval. Responses from third-party APIs are validated like user input, called with timeouts and circuit breakers, and only over TLS to approved hosts.

title: Idempotency keys and duplicate effect prevention
status_rationale: Echelon has no production deployment; the relevant rules exist only in the proposed Secure Construction Standard v0.1 or Unbound requirements, so this is a target state.
target_answer: Every mutating API command requires an idempotency key persisted with a payload hash and the result in the same transaction as the effect. Retries return the stored result; reuse with a different payload is rejected; external effects carry their own idempotency keys to rails and partners; replay of history never re-issues external effects; production effects are reconciled to keys.

challenge.customer_intent: Never pay twice and never lose an instruction.
challenge.adverse_outcome: Duplicate disbursement or grant through a client retry or replayed request.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: Many platforms rely on manual reconciliation and duplicate-detection reports after the fact.
challenge.legally_required: No statute requires idempotency keys; Nacha rules and sponsor fiduciary duties make duplicate payments costly.
challenge.contractually_required: Partners increasingly expect idempotent APIs; not usually a contract term.
challenge.historical_convention: Duplicate payment review and reconciliation exceptions.
challenge.architectural_elimination: Duplicate effects from retries are eliminated within the command layer when key, payload hash and effect share a transaction; external rails still need their own keys and reconciliation.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Command layer rejects missing keys; database uniqueness enforces single use.
challenge.continuous_evidence: Reconciliation of effects to keys; test results per build.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Transactional idempotency plus rail-level keys plus reconciliation, instead of detection only.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Yes through concurrency and replay tests.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Unknown; unvalidated. The prior agent judgment is kept in supporting_arguments.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: Any side effect performed outside the transaction that records the key, or a rail without idempotency support.
challenge.alternative_risks: Key retention windows shorter than retry windows.
supporting_arguments: Prevents rather than detects duplicate payments.
agent judgment: customer acceptance likelihood 'Likely; reconciliation remains expected.'; institutional acceptance rating 'likely' (unvalidated, no cited source).
opposing_arguments: Does not cover rails that lack idempotency; reconciliation is still required.

Institutional acceptance is unvalidated: no buyer, auditor, regulator or insurer evidence or cited source supports an acceptance rating (DD-VAL-ADV-001, DD-VAL-ADV-002). Treat any rating as agent judgment until target-customer conversations or a sourced document support it.

title: API security configuration and agent callers
status_rationale: Echelon has no production deployment; the relevant rules exist only in the proposed Secure Construction Standard v0.1 or Unbound requirements, so this is a target state.
target_answer: API hosts serve TLS only, expose no debug or introspection endpoints, apply a restrictive CORS policy and uniform error format, and are checked daily against a baseline. External and AI agent callers can only submit requests into governed workflows: they cannot approve sponsor-reserved decisions, initiate money movement, modify authoritative events or grant privileges, and each operation publishes a machine-readable contract stating permitted actor types and human approval boundaries.
